title: Inclusionary zoning rates stay as approved
subtitle: Heritage belfry permit, missing middle housing incentives, return envelopes, Centre in the Square appointments, regional water supply concerns
overview: Council rejected a motion to cut inclusionary zoning set-aside rates in the protected major transit station areas from 2% to 0.5% and from 1% to 0.25%. The downtown core portion and the rest of the city were voted on separately, and both were defeated {{vote:m3}} {{vote:m4}}. The rates Council approved a year ago will therefore take effect on January 1, 2026.

Council also approved a Missing Middle and Affordable Housing Community Improvement Plan covering the whole city, and approved a heritage permit for 1385 Bleams Road that requires the belfry to be rebuilt. The owners have said they will appeal that condition to the Ontario Land Tribunal. Other approvals included an eight-storey building near Weber and Young streets, an end to return envelopes with mailed paper bills from February 1, 2026, and new Centre in the Square board appointments.

In closed session Council authorized a long-term land lease at 449-471 Wellington Street North and a lease for food and beverage services at the Cowan Recreation Centre. Under questions, a councillor raised the Region of Waterloo's water supply announcement, and staff said more information would be shared as the Region provides it.

decisions.detail: A motion to reduce set-aside rates to 0.5% and 0.25% for 2026 and 2027 was defeated {{vote:m3}}, so the previously approved rates start January 1, 2026.

decisions.item: Missing Middle and Affordable Housing Community Improvement Plan
decisions.detail: Council designated the whole city as a community improvement project area, approved the plan, and authorized staff to sign related agreements.
Demolition of a shed, two additions and the belfry was approved, with conditions including a heritage easement agreement and restoration or reconstruction of the belfry.

decisions.item: Heritage permit for 50-56 Weber Street West and 107 Young Street
decisions.detail: Council approved demolition of a rear porch and construction of an eight-storey building, subject to heritage review conditions.
The City will stop including return envelopes with mailed paper bills effective February 1, 2026.
Council made board appointments and renewals and adopted a by-law increasing the number of directors from fourteen to fifteen.

Following closed session, Council directed closure of a laneway, declared land surplus, and authorized a long-term lease and a development charge deferral agreement for 449-471 Wellington Street North.
Council transferred $415,000 from Development Charges reserve funds for Roads and Water so the Huron Road project can proceed.

debate: Most delegates on inclusionary zoning opposed the reduction. They said the rates were already low, that a rate of 0.25% would yield about one affordable unit in a building of several hundred, and that incentives and upzoning already benefit developers. Several residents described struggling to find affordable rental housing.

Delegates for the home builders' association and Build Urban supported the reduced rates. They said high-density development is at a standstill and that added costs would delay recovery. They called the motion a compromise that gets the policy started. Staff said the motion would not compromise the Housing Accelerator Fund commitments.

Councillors who supported reduction argued that a policy that stalls projects produces no affordable homes, and that 2% of zero units is still zero. Those opposed said the rules give developers predictability, the City has already made many concessions to the industry, and affordable units are needed now.

At the heritage item, the property owners objected to the belfry reconstruction and the heritage easement, citing cost, doubts about whether the roof could support it, and whether the law requires it. Staff said the easement is temporary and would be removed from title once the work is done. They said a heritage grant could cover up to half the cost, and that the matter would return to Council if the condition proved unworkable.
Under questions, councillors asked the Region for faster, clearer information on a water supply capacity issue. Staff and the Mayor stressed that it concerns water quantity, not quality.
